records.routeTitle: Euclid I.47: area comparisons and constructed squares
records.proofSketch: On the sides of right triangle $ABC$ (right angle at $A$) construct squares $BDEC$, $GB$ and $HC$, and draw $AL$ through $A$ parallel to $BD$. Triangles $ABD$ and $FBC$ are congruent (two sides and the included angle are equal, since both equal a right angle plus $\angle ABC$). The parallelogram $BL$ is double triangle $ABD$ (same base $BD$, same parallels), and the square $GB$ is double triangle $FBC$ (same base $FB$, same parallels), so $BL = GB$. Joining $AE$ and $BK$ gives in the same way $CL = HC$. Hence the square $BDEC$ on the hypotenuse equals $GB + HC$, the sum of the squares on the legs.

records.routeTitle: drop an altitude and use similar triangles
records.proofSketch: Drop the perpendicular from the right-angle vertex to the hypotenuse $c$, cutting it into segments $x$ and $c-x$. The two small triangles and the original triangle have the same angles, so all three are similar. Equal ratios of corresponding sides give $x/a=a/c$ and $(c-x)/b=b/c$, that is $x=a^2/c$ and $c-x=b^2/c$. Adding, $a^2/c+b^2/c=x+(c-x)=c$, and multiplying by $c$ yields $a^2+b^2=c^2$.

records.proofSketch: Take two squares of side $a+b$, each containing four copies of the right triangle with legs $a,b$ and hypotenuse $c$. In one square the triangles are placed so that their hypotenuses enclose a central square of side $c$; its area is $(a+b)^2 = 2ab + c^2$. In the other square the triangles are moved into two $a\times b$ rectangles, leaving two squares of areas $a^2$ and $b^2$, so $(a+b)^2 = 2ab + a^2 + b^2$. Equating and cancelling the area $2ab$ of the four triangles gives $a^2+b^2=c^2$.

records.proofSketch: Assume $\sqrt2=p/q$ with whole numbers $p,q$ having no common factor. Squaring gives $p^2=2q^2$, so $p^2$ is even and hence $p$ is even, say $p=2a$. Then $4a^2=2q^2$, so $q^2=2a^2$ and $q$ is even as well by the same reasoning. Thus $p$ and $q$ share the factor 2, contradicting the choice of lowest terms, so no such $p,q$ exist.

records.routeTitle: infinite descent on a smaller integer pair
records.proofSketch: Suppose $\sqrt2=x/y$ with positive integers; the plan is to produce another fraction $x_1/y_1$ for $\sqrt2$ with $0<y_1<y$, which would give an infinite decreasing sequence of positive denominators. Put $x_1=2y-x$ and $y_1=x-y$. From $x^2=2y^2$ one checks by cross-multiplication that $x/y=(2y-x)/(x-y)$. Also $0<y_1<y$ is equivalent to $y<x<2y$, i.e. $1<(x/y)^2<4$, which holds because $(x/y)^2=2$. So a fraction with smaller denominator exists, contradicting minimality (or well-ordering), and $\sqrt2$ is irrational.

records.routeTitle: geometric descent on an isosceles right triangle
records.proofSketch: Start from an isosceles right triangle with legs $q$ and hypotenuse $p$, both whole numbers, with $p$ taken as small as possible; then $p=\sqrt2 q>q$. By the algebraic proof $p$ is even, so the hypotenuse can be bisected into two lengths $p/2$ and its midpoint joined to the right-angle vertex. This yields two smaller isosceles right triangles each with hypotenuse $q$ and legs $p/2$. The ratio hypotenuse/leg is then $q/(p/2)$ with $q<p$, contradicting minimality of $p$.

records.proofSketch: For primes p≤x expand ∏(1−1/p)⁻¹ into geometric series. Unique factorization includes every reciprocal 1/n for n≤x, so the product is at least Hₓ, which diverges; a finite set of primes would bound the product, contradiction.

records.proofSketch: Let S=Z with the topology generated by all two-sided arithmetic progressions. Each progression is clopen, so any finite union of progressions is closed. Let A be the union of pZ over all primes p. Every integer except −1 and 1 is divisible by a prime, hence Z\A={−1,1}; this two-point set is not open in this topology, so A is not closed. Thus A cannot be a finite union of the closed sets pZ, and there must be infinitely many primes.

records.proofSketch: For s>1, unique factorization gives ζ(s)=∏ₚ(1−p^(−s))⁻¹. If there were finitely many primes, the right side would remain bounded as s↓1, whereas ζ(s)=Σn⁻ˢ diverges by comparison with ∫₁∞x⁻ˢdx. Contradiction. This is an analytic Euler-product proof and overlaps route 3-r2; it is not a distinct strategy unless the ζ-function argument is developed separately.

records.entryName: Infinitely many primes in an arithmetic progression (selected cases)
records.proofSketch: For a fixed modulus m, let P be the finite set of primes dividing m or a₁⋯aₖ. Choose N divisible by m and by all listed primes, and consider aN+1; any prime divisor q is new and q∤aN. This alone controls only q∤m when q is chosen with additional congruence constraints; a general product-plus-one is insufficient to force q≡a (mod m). The route is valid only for specially engineered progressions, as the catalog says.

records.routeTitle: algebraic norms/cyclotomic factors for suitable progressions
records.proofSketch: For a suitable cyclotomic value Φ_n(A), any prime divisor not dividing nA has multiplicative order n modulo q, hence n|(q−1), so q≡1 (mod n). Taking A arbitrarily large yields new such prime divisors; exclude finitely many exceptional divisors by choosing A. This establishes infinitely many primes ≡1 mod n, not arbitrary reduced residue classes.

records.entryName: Arithmetic mean ≥ geometric mean (finite positive case)
records.proofSketch: For positive xᵢ with fixed sum, replacing any unequal pair a,b by their average preserves the sum and increases their product since ((a+b)/2)²−ab=(a−b)²/4≥0. Iterated smoothing (or compactness and the maximizing-pair argument) gives the maximum product when all entries are equal, hence geometric mean≤arithmetic mean.

records.proofSketch: For weights wᵢ>0 with Σwᵢ=1, let g=Πxᵢ^{wᵢ} and tᵢ=xᵢ/g. The inequality log t≤t−1 gives 0=Σwᵢlog tᵢ≤Σwᵢ(tᵢ−1), hence g≤Σwᵢxᵢ. This proves weighted AM–GM; equal weights give the finite unweighted case.

records.routeTitle: trigonometric area formula and cosine law
records.proofSketch: Let K be the area and C the included angle between sides a,b. Then K=ab sin C/2 and c²=a²+b²−2ab cos C. Thus 16K²=4a²b²(1−cos²C)=4a²b²−(a²+b²−c²)²=((a+b)²−c²)(c²−(a−b)²)=16s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c), so K²=s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c).

records.proofSketch: If prime p divides ab but not a, then gcd(p,a)=1. Bézout gives rp+sa=1; multiply by b: rpb+sab=b. Both terms on the right representation are divisible by p, so p|b.

records.routeTitle: Pair each unit with its inverse, leaving ±1
records.proofSketch: Pair each unit x modulo n with its inverse. All pairs cancel in the product of units except self-inverse units; in a prime field the only roots of x²=1 are ±1, so (n−1)!≡−1 (mod prime n). This proof applies to prime n (and for composite n the Wilson congruence generally fails).

records.proofSketch: For pairwise coprime moduli n₁,…,nₖ, put N=∏nᵢ and Nⱼ=N/nⱼ. Choose yⱼ with Nⱼyⱼ≡1 (mod nⱼ), and set x=Σⱼ bⱼNⱼyⱼ. Modulo nᵢ, every summand except the i-th vanishes and the i-th is bᵢ, giving all required congruences. If x and x′ are two solutions, every nⱼ divides x−x′; pairwise coprimality implies N divides x−x′, proving uniqueness modulo N.

records.proofSketch: Parametrize rational points on unit circle x²+y²=1 by intersecting a line of rational slope t through (−1,0): x=(1−t²)/(1+t²), y=2t/(1+t²). Clear denominators to get an integer Pythagorean triple for every integer t.

records.entryName: Euler's polyhedron formula V−E+F=2 (convex polyhedra/planar graphs)
records.routeTitle: Remove edges/faces inductively in a planar graph
records.proofSketch: Induct on the number of faces of a connected planar graph $G$. If $G$ has one face it is acyclic (Jordan curve theorem) and connected, hence a tree with $E=V-1$, so $V-E+F=2$. Otherwise pick an edge $e$ separating two different faces and delete it. Then $e$ appears only once on each adjacent face boundary, so any path through $e$ can be rerouted around one of the faces and the graph stays connected. The deletion lowers both $E$ and $F$ by one, leaving $V-E+F$ unchanged, so the formula follows by induction.

records.entryName: Euler's polyhedron formula V−E+F=2 (convex polyhedra/planar graphs)
records.proofSketch: Triangulate the planar drawing, adding a diagonal to split each nontriangular face; each such operation increases E and F by one and leaves V−E+F unchanged. For a triangulated drawing with at least two interior triangles, the source proves there are at least two removable boundary triangles. Remove them successively: a removal deletes either one edge and one face, or two edges, one face, and one vertex, preserving V−E+F. The process ends at a single triangle, where V−E+F=3−3+2=2.

records.entryName: Euler's polyhedron formula V−E+F=2 (convex polyhedra/planar graphs)
records.proofSketch: The Euler characteristic of a polyhedron's surface is defined as $\chi=V-E+F$. It is a homotopy invariant because it is computed from homology, which is homotopy invariant. A convex polyhedron is homeomorphic to the 3-ball, so its surface is homeomorphic to the 2-sphere, whose Euler characteristic is 2. Hence $V-E+F=2$ for every convex polyhedron.

records.entryName: There are irrational numbers / R is uncountable
records.proofSketch: Let $T$ be the set of infinite binary sequences and suppose $s_1,s_2,\dots$ enumerates it. Build $s$ by taking its $n$-th digit to be the complement of the $n$-th digit of $s_n$. Then $s\in T$ differs from every $s_n$ in the $n$-th place, so $s$ is not in the list, contradicting the assumption that the list is complete. Hence $T$ is uncountable. The uncountability of $\mathbb R$ then follows by injecting $T$ into $\mathbb R$ (reading a sequence as a decimal fraction $0.t$).

records.entryName: There are irrational numbers / R is uncountable
records.routeTitle: nested intervals avoiding a proposed enumeration
records.proofSketch: Given any sequence $x_1,x_2,\dots$ and an interval $[a,b]$, take the first two terms lying in $(a,b)$ as the endpoints $a_1<b_1$, then the first two terms in $(a_1,b_1)$ as $a_2<b_2$, and so on, producing nested open intervals with $a_n$ increasing and $b_n$ decreasing. If the process stops, the last interval contains at most one $x_n$, so another point of it is missing from the sequence. Otherwise let $a_\infty=\lim a_n$, $b_\infty=\lim b_n$. By induction $(a_n,b_n)$ excludes $x_1,\dots,x_{2n}$, so $x_n\notin(a_n,b_n)$. If $a_\infty=b_\infty$ this common point lies in every interval, so it is not on the list; if $a_\infty<b_\infty$ every point of $[a_\infty,b_\infty]$ is missing. Applying this to a supposed enumeration of $[a,b]$ gives the uncountability.

records.entryName: There are irrational numbers / R is uncountable
records.proofSketch: The set $T$ of infinite binary sequences is uncountable by the diagonal argument. To transfer this to the reals, define an injection $f:T\to\mathbb R$ by reading a binary string as a decimal fraction, $f(t)=0.t$, which sends different strings to different numbers. Since $T$ is uncountable, its image is an uncountable subset of $\mathbb R$, so $\mathbb R$ is uncountable. A bijection $T\to\mathbb R$ can then be built by Cantor's method of removing countable subsets.

records.routeTitle: algebraic proof via symmetric polynomials/Galois theory
records.proofSketch: A nonconstant complex polynomial has |P(z)|→∞ as |z|→∞, so |P| attains a global minimum. If the minimum at z₀ were nonzero, write P(z₀+w)=a₀+aₖwᵏ+… with first nonzero k≥1. Choose w so aₖwᵏ/a₀ is small negative real; higher terms are lower order, making |P(z₀+w)|<|a₀|, contradiction.

records.routeTitle: Difference quotients and local area strips for derivative-of-integral
records.proofSketch: For G(t)=∫ₐᵗf(x)dx, the difference quotient is the average value of f over [t,t+h]; continuity makes it tend to f(t), so G′=f. If F′=f, then (F−G)′=0, so F−G is constant and ∫ₐᵇf=F(b)−F(a).

records.routeTitle: subtract the secant line and apply Rolle
records.proofSketch: Let ℓ be the line through (a,f(a)) and (b,f(b)), with slope m=(f(b)−f(a))/(b−a), and set g=f−ℓ. Then g(a)=g(b)=0 and g inherits continuity on [a,b] and differentiability on (a,b). Rolle’s theorem gives g′(c)=0, hence f′(c)=m.

records.routeTitle: polynomial interpolation on eigenvalues (with hypotheses carefully controlled)
records.proofSketch: Triangularize A over an algebraic closure. Every diagonal entry λ is an eigenvalue, so χ_A(t)=∏(t−λᵢ); the triangular matrix χ_A(A) has zero diagonal and is nilpotent, not automatically zero. Therefore this argument alone is insufficient; strengthen with generalized eigenspaces, where (A−λI)^{m_λ}=0 and χ_A contains that factor, to obtain zero on each primary component.

records.proofSketch: For existence, let G act on k-element subsets of itself where |G|=pᵐs and p∤s. The binomial coefficient C(pᵐs,pᵐ) is not divisible by p, so some orbit has size prime to p; its stabilizer has p-part pᵐ and contains a Sylow p-subgroup. For conjugacy, act on cosets G/H; an orbit-count modulo p yields a fixed coset when H is p-subgroup, giving conjugate containment. Conjugation on Sylow subgroups then gives n_p≡1 mod p and n_p||G|.

records.routeTitle: Cyclic rotation acts on p-tuples with product 1
records.proofSketch: Let C_p cyclically rotate p-tuples (g₁,…,g_p) with product 1. There are |G|^(p−1), divisible by p when p||G|. Nonfixed orbits have size p; fixed tuples are (g,…,g) with g^p=1. The fixed-point count is divisible by p and includes identity, so there is a nonidentity element with g^p=1, hence order p.

records.routeTitle: Ratios of subtriangle areas and cancellation around the triangle
records.proofSketch: Signs are handled first: the product of the three signed ratios is positive whether the concurrency point O is inside the triangle or outside. For magnitudes, triangles of equal height have areas proportional to their bases, so |BD|/|DC| = |BOD|/|COD| = |BAD|/|CAD|, and subtracting numerators and denominators gives BD/DC = |ABO|/|CAO| (adding instead if A and O lie on opposite sides of BC). The same argument gives CE/EA = |BCO|/|ABO| and AF/FB = |CAO|/|BCO|. Multiplying the three equations, the area ratios cancel cyclically and the product of the three ratios has absolute value 1.

records.proofSketch: The page states the trigonometric form: sin∠ABE/sin∠CBE · sin∠BCF/sin∠ACF · sin∠CAD/sin∠BAD = 1 for concurrent cevians AD, BE, CF. In its proof, the side-ratio product AF/FB·BD/DC·CE/EA = 1 is rewritten as a product of area ratios of triangles sharing the concurrency point K (e.g. AFK/BFK), since each pair has a common altitude from K. Each area is then written as (1/2)·side·side·sine of the included angle (e.g. AFK = AF·AK·sin∠BAD/2), and the common factors cancel, leaving the product of sine ratios equal to the inverse side-ratio product, hence 1.

records.routeTitle: barycentric coordinates and a determinant condition
records.proofSketch: Let O have barycentric coordinates (λ_A, λ_B, λ_C) with sum 1 and, since O is on no side line, all nonzero. Taking X = F (the intersection of AB and OC), the relation XO = λ_A XA + λ_B XB + λ_C XC rearranges to FO − λ_C FC = λ_A FA + λ_B FB. The left side is parallel to CF and the right side to AB, which are not parallel, so both vanish and λ_A FA + λ_B FB = 0, giving AF/FB = λ_B/λ_A. The same reasoning gives BD/DC = λ_C/λ_B and CE/EA = λ_A/λ_C, and the product is 1.

records.proofSketch: For p = 4n+1, a lemma of Lagrange (or Euler's criterion) supplies an integer m with p | m^2+1. Since Z[i] is Euclidean, hence a UFD, and p divides (m+i)(m−i) but neither factor (their imaginary parts are ±1), p is not prime in Z[i]. So p has a nontrivial factorization, which by multiplicativity of the norm (N(p) = p^2) has exactly two factors, p = (x+yi)(x−yi), and hence p = x^2 + y^2. The first Dedekind proof on the same page uses the Frobenius map on Z[i]/(p) and splitting of the ideal (p) instead.

records.proofSketch: For p = 4m+1, Wilson's theorem gives that n = (2m)! is a square root of −1 modulo p (alternatively n = g^m for a primitive root g). Then p divides n^2+1 = (n+i)(n−i) in Z[i] but neither factor, so p is not irreducible there; to conclude it is not prime, the page shows Z[i] is Euclidean for the norm via a lattice argument, hence a UFD. So p = (a+bi)(c+di) with nonunits, and taking norms gives p^2 = (a^2+b^2)(c^2+d^2) with neither factor 1, so p = a^2+b^2.

records.proofSketch: Since p ≡ 1 mod 4, −1 is a quadratic residue mod p, so p | m^2+1 for some m. Take the lattice S spanned by u = (1,m) and v = (0,p). Any w = au+bv = (a, am+bp) has ||w||^2 ≡ a^2(1+m^2) ≡ 0 mod p. The fundamental parallelogram has area p, while the open disc of radius √(2p) has area 2πp > 4p and is convex and symmetric, so Minkowski's theorem gives a nonzero lattice point in it. Then 0 < ||w||^2 < 2p and p | ||w||^2, so p = ||w||^2 is a sum of two squares.

records.proofSketch: For distinct odd primes p,q, Gauss's lemma says (q/p)=(-1)^N where N counts least positive residues of q,2q,…,((p−1)/2)q that exceed p/2. Counting lattice points in the rectangle 1≤i≤(p−1)/2, 1≤j≤(q−1)/2 below/above the line qi=pj gives N_p+N_q=((p−1)/2)((q−1)/2), yielding (p/q)(q/p)=(-1)^(((p−1)/2)((q−1)/2)).

records.proofSketch: Count lattice points in the rectangle 1≤x≤(p−1)/2, 1≤y≤(q−1)/2 using the line y=(q/p)x; no lattice point lies on it. The two complementary regions are counted by Gauss-lemma exponents for (q/p) and (p/q). Their total count is ((p−1)/2)((q−1)/2), giving quadratic reciprocity's sign.

records.entryName: Fundamental theorem of arithmetic for polynomials over a field
records.proofSketch: For nonzero f,g∈F[x], divide f=qg+r with deg r<deg g. Repeated division terminates by strict degree descent and yields gcd as a linear combination; irreducibles are prime by Bézout, and induction on degree gives factorization and uniqueness up to nonzero constants/order.

records.entryName: Fundamental theorem of arithmetic for polynomials over a field
records.proofSketch: F[x] is a PID by polynomial division. In any UFD, every nonzero nonunit factors into irreducibles by induction on a well-founded size (degree); irreducibles are prime in a PID, so Euclid's lemma gives uniqueness up to units and ordering.

records.entryName: Fundamental theorem of arithmetic for polynomials over a field
records.proofSketch: In an algebraic closure, repeatedly split any reducible polynomial into lower-degree factors until every factor is irreducible; degree strictly decreases, guaranteeing termination. Uniqueness follows because F[x] is a PID and irreducibles there are prime. Algebraic closure is unnecessary for the existence factorization and this route is therefore not as independent as it first appears.

records.routeTitle: linear-algebra nullspace of a Sylvester matrix/resultant
records.proofSketch: For polynomials f,g over a field, a common factor exists exactly when there are nonzero A,B with deg A < deg g and deg B < deg f such that Af+Bg=0. The forward direction uses f=f₁h and g=g₁h, taking A=−g₁, B=f₁. Conversely, if gcd(f,g)=1, Bézout gives Ãf+Ḃg=1; multiplying by B and substituting Bg=−Af forces f to divide B, contradicting deg B<deg f. Writing the bounded-degree relation coefficientwise gives the Sylvester matrix; its determinant is the resultant, which vanishes precisely when this system has a nonzero solution.

records.routeTitle: Expand logarithmic derivative of the generating polynomial
records.proofSketch: Write P(t)=∏(1+x_i t)=∑e_k t^k. Then tP'(t)/P(t)=∑_{m≥1}(-1)^{m-1}p_m t^m, where p_m=∑x_i^m. Multiply by P and compare t^k coefficients to obtain Newton's recurrence.

records.proofSketch: Form the weighted set of pairs (A,j^l), where A is a subset of {1,…,n}, j is an index, |A|+l=k, and l=0 requires j∈A. Give each pair weight (−1)^|A|(∏_{i∈A}x_i)x_j^l. Their total weight is the Newton recurrence. Toggle j's membership in A, adjusting l by one; this is a weight-reversing involution, so all terms cancel.

records.proofSketch: Use indicator functions, noting 1_A·1_B = 1_{A∩B}. For the union A of A_1,...,A_n, one wants 1_A = Σ_{k≥1}(−1)^{k−1} Σ_{|I|=k} 1_{A_I}, where A_I is the intersection over I. The product (1_A − 1_{A_1})···(1_A − 1_{A_n}) vanishes identically: at a point outside A every factor is 0 − 0, and at a point of some A_m the m-th factor is 1 − 1. Expanding the product gives the identity. Summing over x (or taking expectations, or integrating) gives the cardinality, probability, or measure form by linearity.

records.routeTitle: classify elements by exact membership set
records.proofSketch: Theorem 2.1.1 shows that the operator φ f(T) = Σ_{Y⊇T} f(Y) on functions on subsets of S is invertible with φ^{-1} f(T) = Σ_{Y⊇T}(−1)^{#(Y−T)} f(Y); this is checked by composing and using Σ_{i}(−1)^i C(m,i) = δ_{0m}. In the combinatorial setting, f_=(T) counts objects having exactly the properties in T and f_≥(T) those having at least T, so f_≥(T) = Σ_{Y⊇T} f_=(Y) (2.3). Inverting gives f_=(T) = Σ_{Y⊇T}(−1)^{#(Y−T)} f_≥(Y) (2.4), and taking T = ∅ counts objects having none of the properties (2.5).

records.routeTitle: Möbius inversion on the Boolean lattice
records.proofSketch: The Boolean algebra B_n is the product of n copies of the 2-chain, so by the product theorem for Möbius functions μ(T,S) = (−1)^{#(S−T)}. Möbius inversion on B_n then says g(S) = Σ_{T⊆S} f(T) for all S iff f(S) = Σ_{T⊆S}(−1)^{#(S−T)} g(T), which is equation (2.8), the inclusion-exclusion principle. The direct check of the inverse is in the proof of Theorem 2.1.1: in the composite φψ, the coefficient of f(Z) is Σ_{T⊆Y⊆Z}(−1)^{#(Y−T)} = δ, so ψ = φ^{-1}.

records.proofSketch: Encode a labelled tree by repeatedly deleting its least-labelled leaf and recording its neighbor; after n−2 deletions the recorded labels form a word of length n−2. To invert, scan the word from left to right, joining its first entry to the least label not appearing in the remaining word, deleting that label and the first entry at each step; finally join the two remaining labels. The procedures are inverse, so labelled trees correspond bijectively to the n^(n−2) words.

records.proofSketch: Let T(x) count rooted labeled trees as an exponential generating function. Decomposing a rooted tree into its root and an unordered set of rooted branches gives T=x exp(T). Lagrange inversion yields [x^n]T=n^(n−1)/n!, so there are n^(n−1) rooted labeled trees; forgetting the choice of root divides by n and gives n^(n−2).

records.entryName: König's theorem (bipartite vertex cover = maximum matching)
records.proofSketch: Formulate bipartite matching as the LP maximizing Σ_e x_e subject to incident-edge sums at each vertex ≤1 and x≥0; the dual minimizes Σ_v y_v subject to y_u+y_v≥1 on each edge and y≥0. The bipartite incidence matrix is totally unimodular, so optimal basic solutions of both programs are integral. The integral primal solution is a matching and the integral dual solution is a vertex cover. Strong LP duality makes their cardinalities equal, proving König’s theorem.

records.routeTitle: Minimal-counterexample vertex of degree ≤5 plus recoloring
records.proofSketch: Choose a vertex v of degree at most five (Euler’s formula guarantees one), color G−v with five colors. If its five neighbors use all colors, relabel cyclically and consider the 1/3 Kempe chain from the first to third neighbor. If they connect, the 2/4 chain cannot connect without crossing; swap one chain and free a color. If they do not connect, swap the 1/3 component. Color v.

records.entryName: Central limit theorem (classical iid finite variance)
records.proofSketch: First truncate the finite-variance summands at a fixed level and recenter them; the normalized tail sum has variance as small as desired, uniformly in n. For bounded summands, expand each fixed moment of the normalized sum: singleton indices vanish, and pairings give the Gaussian moments. Moment determinacy gives convergence for the bounded variables. Let the truncation level grow to obtain the finite-variance theorem.

records.proofSketch: Assume a complete metric space M is the union of closed sets C_n, each with empty interior. records.entryName: Riesz representation theorem for Hilbert spaces
records.proofSketch: For a nonzero bounded functional f on a Hilbert space, ker(f) is a closed subspace and its orthogonal complement is one-dimensional. Choose nonzero x₀ in ker(f)⊥ and set z_f=f(x₀)x₀/||x₀||² (adjusting conjugation for the inner-product convention). On ker(f), both f and ⟨z_f,·⟩ vanish; on ker(f)⊥, which is spanned by x₀, they agree by construction. Hence f(x)=⟨z_f,x⟩ for all x.

records.entryName: Open mapping theorem for Banach spaces
records.proofSketch: It suffices to show T(B_X(0,1)) contains a neighborhood of 0. Surjectivity gives Y=⋃_n T(B_X(0,n)); Baire implies the closure of one such image has interior. By linearity and subtraction this yields a ball around 0 contained in the closure of T(B_X(0,1)). Repeatedly approximate a target y by T(x₁), then its residual by T(x₂), with ||x_k|| geometrically decreasing. The sum converges in X and maps to y, so a neighborhood of 0 lies in T(B_X(0,1)); scaling and translation show T is open.

records.proofSketch: Prove the theorem first for a triangle C. Joining midpoints of the sides splits C into four positively oriented triangles whose interior edges cancel, so the integral over C is the sum of the four integrals, and one of them, C_1, has modulus at least a quarter of the total. Iterating gives nested triangles C_n with $|\int_C f| \le 4^n |\int_{C_n} f|$, shrinking to a point $z_0$ where f is differentiable. Writing $f(z)=f(z_0)+f'(z_0)(z-z_0)+\eta(z)(z-z_0)$ with $\eta\to 0$, the linear part integrates to zero over the closed triangle, so $\int_{C_n} f=\int_{C_n}\eta(z)(z-z_0)\,dz$. Since $L_n=2^{-n}L$ and $|z-z_0|<L_n/2$, the estimate gives $|\int_C f|\le\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon$, hence zero. Polygons follow by triangulating, and general simple closed contours by polygonal approximation (details omitted in the source).

records.proofSketch: Assume additionally that $f'$ is continuous. Writing $f=u+iv$, the contour integral splits as $\int_C u\,dx - v\,dy + i\int_C v\,dx+u\,dy$. Green's theorem turns the real part into $\iint_R(-v_x-u_y)\,dx\,dy$ and the imaginary part into $\iint_R(u_x-v_y)\,dx\,dy$, where R is the interior of C. The Cauchy-Riemann equations $u_x=v_y$, $u_y=-v_x$ make both integrands zero, so $\int_C f\,dz=0$.

records.routeTitle: homotopy/primitive arguments on simply connected domains
records.proofSketch: For f analytic on a simply connected domain D, fix $z_0$ and set $F(z)=\int_{z_0}^z f(\xi)\,d\xi$. Path independence: two contours $C_1,C_2$ from $z_0$ to $z$ give a closed contour $C_1-C_2$ whose integral vanishes by the Cauchy-Goursat theorem, so F is well defined. For the derivative, $F(z+\Delta z)-F(z)=\int_\Gamma f$ over the segment from z to $z+\Delta z$, and since $\int_\Gamma f(z)\,d\xi=f(z)\Delta z$, continuity of f gives $|(F(z+\Delta z)-F(z))/\Delta z - f(z)|<\varepsilon$. Hence $F'=f$.

records.routeTitle: finite-field cyclicity as the finite-field special case
records.proofSketch: A finite subgroup of a field's multiplicative group is cyclic: for each divisor d, roots of X^d−1 are at most d, which forces the group exponent to equal its order; an element of full order exists in a finite abelian group. Thus every finite field extension is generated by a primitive element. This only treats finite fields.

records.entryName: Stone's representation theorem for Boolean algebras
records.proofSketch: For Boolean algebra B, let X be ultrafilters, and set U_b={u:b∈u}. These clopen sets satisfy Boolean operations and separate ultrafilters; compactness follows because any cover without finite subcover yields a family with finite intersection property extendable to an ultrafilter. Thus B≅Clop(X).

records.entryName: Nielsen–Schreier theorem (subgroups of free groups are free)

records.routeTitle: Differential forms and local Poincaré lemma with partitions of unity
records.proofSketch: Consider the complex of sheaves $0\to\mathbb{R}_M\to\Omega^0_M\xrightarrow{d}\Omega^1_M\to\cdots$. The Poincaré lemma says closed forms are locally exact, so this sequence of sheaves is exact. Each $\Omega^k_M$ is fine, because local sections can be glued by a partition of unity (multiply by the partition functions and sum), and a fine sheaf has vanishing higher Čech cohomology by an explicit homotopy built from the partition of unity. Hence the sequence is a fine resolution of the constant sheaf, and the cohomology of its global sections, namely de Rham cohomology, equals the Čech (sheaf) cohomology of $\mathbb{R}_M$.

records.proofSketch: Call a manifold de Rham if the integration map $H^p_{dR}(M)\to H^p(M;\mathbb R)$ is an isomorphism, and a cover a de Rham cover if its members and all their finite intersections are de Rham. Disjoint unions of de Rham manifolds are de Rham, and convex open sets in $\mathbb R^n$ are de Rham by the Poincaré lemma and homotopy invariance. For a finite de Rham cover, induct on the number of sets: compare the Mayer-Vietoris sequences of de Rham and singular cohomology for $U=U_1\cup\dots\cup U_k$ and $V=U_{k+1}$, and conclude with the five lemma. For a de Rham basis, an exhaustion function splits $M$ into two disjoint unions of finitely covered pieces, whose union and intersection are de Rham. Open subsets of $\mathbb R^n$, hence every manifold, have such a basis of balls.

records.proofSketch: Define a fine resolution of a sheaf $\mathcal F$ as an exact sequence $0\to\mathcal F\to\mathcal F^0\to\mathcal F^1\to\cdots$ with every $\mathcal F^k$ fine. Theorem 4.5 compares the Čech cohomology of a good cover with the cohomology of the complex of global sections of the resolution by chasing a double complex: rows below the first are exact because the $\mathcal F^k$ are fine, columns are exact by the hypothesis on the cover. Passing to the limit over covers (Leray) gives that the cohomology of $\mathcal F$ equals that of the global sections complex of any fine resolution. Applied to $0\to\mathbb{R}_M\to\Omega^0_M\to\Omega^1_M\to\cdots$, a fine resolution by the Poincaré lemma and partitions of unity, this identifies sheaf cohomology of $\mathbb{R}_M$ with de Rham cohomology.

records.proofSketch: Use Cartan's formula $L_\xi=d\,i(\xi)+i(\xi)d$. For a family of maps $f_t$ with velocity field $\xi_t$, differentiate $f_t^*\omega$ to get $\frac{d}{dt}f_t^*\omega=f_t^*L_{\xi_t}\omega$. Integrate over $t\in[0,1]$ and apply Cartan's formula to obtain $f_1^*\omega-f_0^*\omega=dJ\omega+Jd\omega$ with $J\omega=\int_0^1 f_t^*i(\xi_t)\omega\,dt$. On a ball centred at $x_0$ take the radial contraction $f_t(x)=t(x-x_0)+x_0$, so $f_1^*\omega=\omega$ and $f_0^*\omega=0$ for forms of positive degree; hence $\omega=dJ\omega$ when $d\omega=0$.

records.proofSketch: For a star-shaped open $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ consider forms on $U\times[0,1]$ and define fiber integration $\pi_*$ by integrating the coefficient of $dt$ over $[0,1]$. Differentiation under the integral sign gives $\pi_*(d\alpha)=\alpha_1-\alpha_0-d(\pi_*\alpha)$. Pull back along the straight-line contraction $h(x,t)=tx$ and set $J=\pi_*\circ h^*$ to obtain the homotopy formula $h_1^*\omega-h_0^*\omega=Jd\omega+dJ\omega$. For closed $\omega$ of positive degree, $h_1^*\omega=\omega$ and $h_0^*\omega=0$, so $\omega=dJ\omega$.

records.proofSketch: The symmetric strict inequality $|f-g|<|f|+|g|$ on $\partial K$ implies $f,g$ have no zeros there and $g$ is never a negative real multiple of $f$. By the argument principle $N_f(K)$ equals the winding number of $f\circ C$ about $0$, and likewise for $g$. The segment homotopy $H_t=(1-t)f\circ C+t\,g\circ C$ avoids the origin, and the winding number $I(t)=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_{H_t}dz/z$ is continuous and integer-valued, hence constant. So $N_f(K)=N_g(K)$. The usual form $|g|<|f|$ follows by applying this to $f+g$ and $f$.

records.entryName: Poincaré duality for closed oriented manifolds
records.proofSketch: Hatcher motivates Poincaré duality with dual cell structures C and C* on a closed manifold: each i-cell of C is dual to a unique (n-i)-cell of C* meeting it transversally in one point. Pairing cells with dual cells identifies the cellular chain groups C_i with C*_{n-i}. With Z_2 coefficients this identification is canonical, and the cellular boundary of C becomes the coboundary of C*, since boundary sends a cell to the sum of its faces while coboundary sends it to the sum of cells it is a face of. Hence H_i(C;Z_2) is isomorphic to H^{n-i}(C*;Z_2), and since C and C* are cell structures on the same space, H_i(M;Z_2) is isomorphic to H^{n-i}(M;Z_2). For Z coefficients one must choose compatible orientations of all cells when M is orientable. Hatcher treats this only as a sketch (worked for surfaces, then stated for dimension n) and abandons it, because constructing dual cell structures for general manifolds needs more manifold theory.

records.entryName: Poincaré duality for closed oriented manifolds
records.proofSketch: Hatcher proves the stronger statement that the duality map D_M: H^k_c(M;R) -> H_{n-k}(M;R), x -> mu_K cap x (limit over compact K), is an isomorphism for every R-oriented n-manifold; for closed M it is cap product with the fundamental class. The key technical lemma gives a commutative-up-to-sign map between the Mayer-Vietoris sequences for compactly supported cohomology and for homology, built from excision and the classes mu_K, so by the five-lemma D_{U cup V} is an isomorphism if D_U, D_V, D_{U cap V} are. A direct-limit argument handles increasing unions of open sets. The base case M = R^n is read off from cap product on (Delta^n, boundary of Delta^n). One then passes to open subsets of R^n by induction over covers by convex sets, to manifolds that are countable unions of Euclidean opens, and in general by Zorn's lemma using a maximal open set on which duality holds.

records.entryName: Poincaré duality for closed oriented manifolds
records.proofSketch: Work with oriented M and the integration pairing H^q(M) x H^{n-q}_c(M) -> R, [w],[t] -> integral of w ^ t. The Mayer-Vietoris sequence of de Rham cohomology and the one for compactly supported cohomology (in reverse order) are linked by this integration pairing; the Main Lemma checks, square by square, that the pairings commute up to sign (the connecting-map square is the delicate one, comparing integrals of df_V ^ w ^ t). For M = R^n the Poincare lemmas leave only the pairing of constants with compactly supported top forms, which is obviously nondegenerate. The five lemma then shows that nondegeneracy for U, V and U cap V gives it for U cup V, and induction over a finite good cover (all intersections diffeomorphic to R^n) yields the result for manifolds with a finite good cover, in particular compact ones; finite dimensionality turns it into an isomorphism.

records.entryName: Poincaré duality for closed oriented manifolds
records.proofSketch: Define Morse cohomology with the pair (-f,g) instead of (f,g): the chain groups are again generated by the critical points of f, but since negating f turns the index p of a critical point into n-p and reverses flow lines, the Morse differential becomes an ascending coboundary delta of degree +1 counting flow lines. Because -f has the same critical points as f, C_i is isomorphic to C^{n-i}, and this identification intertwines the boundary and coboundary maps, giving MH^{n-*}(X) = MH_*(X) for the Morse (co)homology. Torres interprets this as 'looking at X upside down does not change its homology'. The argument is compressed and does not discuss orientations or the handle/intersection-pairing picture.

records.entryName: Poincaré duality for closed oriented manifolds
records.proofSketch: On a compact oriented Riemannian n-manifold, the Hodge star is defined by alpha ^ *beta = (alpha, beta) dvol and satisfies ** = +-1, giving the L^2 inner product <alpha,beta> = integral of alpha ^ *beta. By the Hodge theorem every de Rham class has a unique norm-minimising (harmonic) representative. The star maps harmonic i-forms isomorphically onto harmonic (n-i)-forms, so H^i and H^{n-i} have the same dimension. For the integration pairing, the induced map H^i -> (H^{n-i})* has zero kernel because the pairing of a nonzero harmonic alpha with *alpha is the squared norm, hence nonzero; equal dimensions then give a perfect pairing.

records.entryName: Szemerédi's theorem (positive-density subsets of integers contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions)
records.proofSketch: Apply Szemerédi regularity to a graph built from a dense set, then use the counting lemma and van der Waerden-type structure to force a long progression; the energy-increment/regularity argument rules out a progression-free positive-density set.

records.entryName: Szemerédi's theorem (positive-density subsets of integers contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions)
records.proofSketch: Encode a dense set A⊂[N] by a shift system and its indicator. The correspondence principle turns progressions into multiple recurrence; Furstenberg’s recurrence theorem gives positive measure to ⋂_{j=0}^{k−1}T^{−jn}B for some n, and the correspondence transfers this to a k-term progression in A.

Decompose f into structured and uniform parts; generalized von Neumann bounds the uniform contribution by a Gowers uniformity norm, while an inverse theorem gives structure and density increment until density exceeds 1.

records.proofSketch: Encode k-term progressions as edges in a multipartite hypergraph. Hypergraph regularity plus a counting lemma forces a configuration in any positive-density set; equivalently, density Hales–Jewett yields combinatorial lines, which map to progressions. The original theorem and density-HJ are related formulations, not literally identical statements.

records.entryName: Hook-length formula for standard Young tableaux
records.proofSketch: Run the Greene–Nijenhuis–Wilf hook walk from an outside corner: at each cell choose uniformly among cells strictly to its left or above in its hook, then move to the chosen cell. Compute the probability of terminating at each removable corner; the resulting recurrence matches the tableau count f^λ=|λ|!/∏h(c), with the hook factors emerging from transition probabilities.

records.proofSketch: Assume every finite subset of the first-order theory T has a model. Expand the language in countably many stages by fresh constants witnessing each existential formula, while preserving finite satisfiability. The resulting Henkin theory has a model built from closed terms modulo provable equality: interpret functions on term classes and relations by membership in the theory. Its reduct satisfies T.

records.proofSketch: Let I be the finite subsets of Γ and choose a model A_i of each i. For each finite i let J_i={j∈I:i⊆j}; these cones have the finite-intersection property, so extend their generated filter to an ultrafilter U. In the ultraproduct Π_i A_i/U, for each φ∈Γ the indices whose structures satisfy φ include J_{ {φ} }, hence form a U-large set. Łoś’s theorem gives that the ultraproduct satisfies every φ.

records.proofSketch: Let f be the minimal polynomial over Q of a primitive n-th root ζ. For a prime p∤n, suppose ζ^p is not a conjugate; let g be its distinct minimal polynomial. Then f and g are distinct monic integer factors of X^n−1. Modulo p, Frobenius gives the relevant pth-power relation between roots, forcing a repeated factor of X^n−1; this is impossible because p∤n makes X^n−1 square-free mod p. Thus ζ and ζ^p are conjugate. Factoring any a coprime to n into primes not dividing n and iterating shows every ζ^a is conjugate to ζ, so Φ_n is irreducible over Q.

records.routeTitle: reduction modulo a prime and Frobenius
records.proofSketch: For p∤n, every root α of Φ_n over F_p is a primitive n-th root: otherwise it would also be a root of X^d−1 for a proper divisor d|n, contradicting separability of X^n−1. Frobenius α↦α^p has orbit length ord_n(p), so each irreducible factor of Φ_n mod p has degree ord_n(p). Consequently Φ_n mod p is irreducible exactly when p mod n generates (Z/nZ)^×. This is a conditional modular criterion; such a prime need not exist for every n.

records.proofSketch: Count monotone N/E walks with n N's and n E's that never have more E's than N's. Total walks number $\binom{2n}{n}$, so subtract the bad walks. For a bad walk, find the first step at which E's outnumber N's; interchange N and E in the segment up to and including that step. The result has $n+1$ N's and $n-1$ E's, and the map is reversible (first time N's exceed E's), so bad walks are in bijection with all walks in an $(n-1)\times(n+1)$ grid. Hence $C_n=\binom{2n}{n}-\binom{2n}{n-1}=\frac1{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$.

records.proofSketch: Take a nonempty Dyck path and look at the first time after the initial up step that it returns to the diagonal, at $(k,k)$. Removing the first and last steps of the initial excursion leaves a Dyck path of semilength $k-1$, and the remainder is a Dyck path of semilength $n-k$; thus $C_n=\sum_{k=1}^nC_{k-1}C_{n-k}$ with $C_0=1$. Multiplying the recurrence by $x^n$ and summing gives $(C(x)-1)/x=C(x)^2$, i.e. $xC^2-C+1=0$; the minus sign in the quadratic formula is forced by $C(0)=1$, so $C(x)=(1-\sqrt{1-4x})/(2x)$. Extracting coefficients with the binomial series for $(1-4x)^{1/2}$ gives $C_n=\frac1{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$.

records.proofSketch: Show that triangulations of a polygon with $n+2$ sides (into $n$ triangles) satisfy the Catalan recursion. Fix a side as the base; in any triangulation it lies in exactly one triangle, the base triangle. That triangle splits the polygon into two smaller triangulated polygons, with $k+2$ sides on one side and $n-k+1$ sides on the other, with $k$ running over $0,\dots,n-1$ (extreme values when the base triangle uses two polygon edges). Hence $T_n=\sum_k T_kT_{n-1-k}$ with the same initial values, so $T_n=C_n$.

records.proofSketch: Let $C_n$ count the bracketings of a product of $n$ terms under a non-associative operation. The last application of the operation combines a bracketed product of the first $m$ terms with one of the last $n-m$ terms, giving $C_n=\sum_{m=1}^{n-1}C_mC_{n-m}$ with $C_1=1$. Hence $c(x)=x+c(x)^2$, solved by $c(x)=\tfrac12(1-\sqrt{1-4x})$ (sign fixed by $c(0)=0$); the binomial series gives $C_n=\frac1n\binom{2n-2}{n-1}$ (i.e. $\frac1{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$ for $n+1$ terms). Binary trees with $n$ leaves are parse trees of bracketed products, so they obey the same count.

records.proofSketch: Label a triangulated d-simplex Sperner-style. Count incidences between small d-simplices and their facets labeled {0,…,d−1}; interior facets contribute twice and cancel mod 2, while boundary facets reduce to the (d−1)-dimensional boundary simplex. The remaining parity forces an odd, hence nonzero, number of fully labeled d-simplices.

records.proofSketch: For each sequence position k, let f(k) be the length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at a_k. If any f(k)=n+1, the theorem follows. Otherwise f takes at most n values among n²+1 positions, so n+1 positions k₁<⋯<kₙ₊₁ share one value. Their entries must be strictly decreasing: if i<j and a_{k_i}<a_{k_j}, an increasing subsequence ending at k_i extends to k_j, contradicting equal f-values.

records.proofSketch: Order pairs of rank data (longest increasing ending at i, longest decreasing ending at i). Distinct sequence entries make these pairs distinct: if i<j and a_i<a_j the increasing rank grows; if a_i>a_j the decreasing rank grows. With no monotone subsequence of length r or s, only (r−1)(s−1) rank pairs exist.

records.routeTitle: Euler product and divergence of the harmonic series
records.proofSketch: For each x, the finite Euler product P_x=∏_{p≤x}(1−1/p)^{-1} expands as a sum over integers whose prime factors are at most x, so P_x≥H_x and is unbounded. If Σ_p 1/p converged, then log P_x=Σ_{p≤x}log(1+1/(p−1)) would stay bounded, since log(1+u)≤u and 1/(p−1)≤2/p for p≥2. Thus P_x would be bounded, contradiction; hence Σ_p1/p diverges. This follows the source’s Euler-product/harmonic-series argument, using the corrected harmless constant bound for the logarithm.

records.proofSketch: Assume ∑_p1/p converges and choose y so the tail sum over p>y is <1/2. Integers ≤x with a prime factor >y are at most x∑_{p>y,p≤x}1/p<x/2; those with all prime factors among the finitely many primes ≤y are O((log x)^k)=o(x). These cannot account for all x integers, contradiction.

records.routeTitle: Integrate powers of sine/cosine and use recurrence
records.proofSketch: Set I_m=∫_0^{π/2}sin^m x dx. Integration by parts gives I_m=(m−1)I_{m−2}/m, with I_0=π/2, I_1=1. Since sin^{2n+1}≤sin^{2n}≤sin^{2n−1}, recurrence and a squeeze give (2·4···2n)/(1·3···(2n−1))∼√(πn), equivalent to Wallis’ product.

records.proofSketch: Put c_n=C(2n,n)/4ⁿ=(2n−1)!!/(2n)!!. The Wallis partial product is P_n=∏_{k≤n}(2k)²/((2k−1)(2k+1))=1/((2n+1)c_n²), so the product equals π/2 exactly when c_n∼1/√(πn). That asymptotic follows from Stirling's formula applied to (2n)!/(n!)², giving C(2n,n)∼4ⁿ/√(πn). Caveat: if Stirling's constant √(2π) is itself obtained from Wallis' product the argument is circular, so the constant needs an independent derivation (for instance from the Gaussian integral).

records.proofSketch: Evaluate I_m=∫_0^{π/2}sin^m x dx as a Beta integral: I_m=½B((m+1)/2,½)=(√π/2)Γ((m+1)/2)/Γ(m/2+1). Using Γ(n+½)=(2n−1)!!√π/2ⁿ and Γ(n+1)=n!, the ratio I_{2n+1}/I_{2n} equals (2/π)P_n, where P_n is the n-th Wallis partial product. Since I_{2n+1}/I_{2n}→1 (monotonicity of I_m in m, or log-convexity of Γ), P_n→π/2.

records.routeTitle: Bernstein polynomials and probabilistic binomial concentration
records.proofSketch: For continuous f on [0,1], let B_n f be its Bernstein polynomial. Uniform continuity gives |f(x)−f(a)|≤ε when |x−a|≤δ; elsewhere bound it by 2M(x−a)²/δ², where M=||f||∞. Positivity and linearity of B_n then bound |B_nf(a)−f(a)| by ε plus (2M/δ²)B_n[(x−a)²](a). The Bernstein second-moment identity gives B_n[(x−a)²](a)=a(1−a)/n≤1/(4n), uniformly in a; hence B_nf→f uniformly.

records.proofSketch: Fix a simply connected region Ω≠ℂ and z₀∈Ω and maximize |f′(z₀)| over the univalent maps Ω→D. The family is nonempty (a square-root branch of z−a, with the two branches having disjoint images, composed with an inversion) and the derivative is bounded by the Cauchy estimate. Take a maximizing sequence; the family is bounded by 1, so Montel gives a locally uniformly convergent subsequence, and Hurwitz makes the limit univalent since its derivative at z₀ is nonzero. Composing with a disc automorphism shows the maximizer sends z₀ to 0, and rotating makes f′(z₀)>0. If f(Ω)≠D, a univalent map g on f(Ω) with g(0)=0 and |g′(0)|>1 (Lecture 17) gives g∘f with larger derivative, a contradiction, so f is onto. Uniqueness follows from the Schwarz lemma.

records.entryName: Montel's theorem (locally bounded holomorphic families are normal)
records.proofSketch: Local boundedness gives uniform equicontinuity on compact sets (Cauchy estimates, proved in the previous lecture). On each compact K, Arzelà–Ascoli then gives a subsequence converging uniformly on K. Taking an exhaustion K₁⊂K₂⊂… by compact sets, successively extract subsequences converging uniformly on K₁, K₂, … and take the diagonal sequence, which converges uniformly on every compact set. The limit is holomorphic as a locally uniform limit of holomorphic functions.

records.entryName: Montel's theorem (locally bounded holomorphic families are normal)
records.proofSketch: Use equicontinuity only to upgrade pointwise convergence. Cauchy's estimate bounds |f′| by M/r on D(a,r) whenever |f|≤M on D(a,2r), so a locally bounded family is locally equi-Lipschitz. Diagonalize over a countable dense subset of Ω to get a subsequence converging at each of those points; local equicontinuity then makes it uniformly Cauchy on each compact set. The locally uniform limit is holomorphic by Weierstrass' theorem (or Morera's theorem).

records.entryName: Existence and uniqueness theorem for ODEs (Picard–Lindelöf)
records.proofSketch: Rewrite y′=F(t,y), y(t₀)=y₀ as y(t)=y₀+∫_{t₀}^tF(s,y(s))ds. On a cylinder |t−t₀|≤a, |y−y₀|≤b where F is continuous, |F|≤M and F is L-Lipschitz in y, the integral operator maps C([t₀−h,t₀+h], B̄_b(y₀)) into itself for h≤min(a,b/M), and is a contraction for h<1/L (or in the weighted norm sup e^{−2L|t−t₀|}|u| for the full h). Banach's fixed-point theorem gives a unique solution on that interval, and the Picard iterates converge uniformly to it.

records.entryName: Existence and uniqueness theorem for ODEs (Picard–Lindelöf)
records.routeTitle: Peano polygonal approximations plus equicontinuity for existence
records.proofSketch: Existence needs only continuity of F. On the cylinder with |F|≤M, build Euler polygons y_k with step 1/k on [t₀,t₀+h], h=min(a,b/M). They are uniformly bounded and M-Lipschitz, so Arzelà–Ascoli gives a uniformly convergent subsequence. Uniform continuity of F lets one pass to the limit in y_k(t)=y₀+∫F(s,y_k(s))ds+o(1), which yields a solution; the same works backward in time. This route gives existence without uniqueness (compare y′=√|y|), so the Lipschitz hypothesis enters only through a separate uniqueness step.

records.entryName: Existence and uniqueness theorem for ODEs (Picard–Lindelöf)
records.proofSketch: Uniqueness: let y,z solve the problem on a common interval J∋t₀, and let K be a compact subinterval on which both stay in a set where F is L-Lipschitz in y. Then u=|y−z| satisfies u(t)≤L|∫_{t₀}^t u|, and Gronwall's inequality gives u≡0 on K. Local Lipschitz continuity makes the set {y=z} open (apply the argument near any coincidence point) and continuity makes it closed, so y=z on all of J by connectedness. Paired with an existence step (Picard iteration or Peano), this gives the local existence-and-uniqueness theorem.

records.proofSketch: Assume a=‖f‖_p and b=‖g‖_p are positive (otherwise the claim is trivial) and normalize F=f/a, G=g/b. Then f+g=(a+b)(λF+(1−λ)G) with λ=a/(a+b). Young's inequality xy≤x^p/p+y^q/q is the same convexity (weighted AM–GM) and is what underlies Hölder in the other route.

records.routeTitle: interpolate from the triangle inequality for simple functions and pass by approximation
records.proofSketch: First take simple functions s,t on a common finite measurable partition E_1,…,E_N: then ‖s+t‖_p=(Σμ(E_j)|s_j+t_j|^p)^{1/p} is a weighted ℓ^p norm on ℝ^N, where Minkowski is the finite-sum inequality. For general f,g choose simple 0≤s_n↑|f| and 0≤t_n↑|g|; then ‖s_n+t_n‖_p≤‖s_n‖_p+‖t_n‖_p≤‖f‖_p+‖g‖_p, and monotone convergence gives ‖|f|+|g|‖_p≤‖f‖_p+‖g‖_p, which dominates ‖f+g‖_p. The finite-dimensional inequality still needs its own proof (convexity or Hölder), so this route reduces the problem rather than replacing the argument.

records.proofSketch: Treat L as a Daniell integral on the vector lattice C(K). Dini's theorem makes it continuous from below along decreasing sequences: if f_n↓0 pointwise on compact K then f_n→0 uniformly, so L(f_n)→0. Daniell's extension then gives an integral on a larger class of functions (monotone limits, then upper and lower integrals) and hence a measure on the σ-algebra it generates with L(f)=∫f dμ; since 1∈C(K), the measure is finite. Caveat: this first produces a Baire measure, and regularity on all Borel sets for non-metrizable K needs a further extension argument.

records.entryName: Prokhorov's theorem (tightness and relative compactness of probability measures on Polish spaces)
records.routeTitle: Compactness via finite partitions and diagonal subsequences
records.proofSketch: Given a tight family, pick compacts $K_1\subset K_2\subset\dots$ with $P_n(K_i)>1-i^{-1}$ for all $n$. The union $K_\infty$ is separable, so there is a countable class of open sets whose closures refine any open neighbourhood; form the countable class $\mathcal H$ of finite unions of $\bar A\cap K_i$. A diagonal argument gives a subsequence along which $\alpha(H)=\lim P_{n'}(H)$ exists for every $H\in\mathcal H$. Define $\beta(G)=\sup_{H\subset G}\alpha(H)$ on open sets and $\gamma(M)=\inf_{G\supset M}\beta(G)$. Seven steps show $\gamma$ is an outer measure for which closed sets are measurable and whose restriction $P$ is a probability measure (mass 1 because $K_i\in\mathcal H$), with $P(G)=\beta(G)\le\liminf P_{n'}(G)$ for open $G$, hence weak convergence.

records.proofSketch: For the converse (relative compactness implies tightness on a complete separable metric space): first show that for open sets $G_n\uparrow S$ and $\epsilon>0$ some $n$ has $P(G_n)>1-\epsilon$ for all $P$ in the family, otherwise a weakly convergent subsequence $P_{n'}\Rightarrow Q$ would give $Q(G_n)\le\liminf P_{n'}(G_n)\le1-\epsilon$ for all $n$, impossible. Cover $S$ by balls of radius $1/k$, choose finitely many with mass $>1-\epsilon2^{-k}$, and take the closure of the totally bounded intersection over $k$: it is compact by completeness and has mass $>1-\epsilon$.

records.routeTitle: transport through distribution functions in R
records.proofSketch: Helly selection on the line: enumerate the rationals and by diagonalisation extract a subsequence of distribution functions converging at every rational to some $G$; set $G(x)=\inf\{G(q):q>x\}$, which is right-continuous and nondecreasing, and convergence at continuity points follows from convergence at rationals. Tightness ($\limsup_n 1-F_n(M_\epsilon)+F_n(-M_\epsilon)\le\epsilon$) is exactly the condition that every subsequential limit is a probability distribution function, ruling out escape of mass; this last equivalence is only cited, not proved, in the source.

records.proofSketch: For finite $\mu$ and finite positive $\lambda$, put $\phi=\lambda+\mu$. The functional $f\mapsto\lambda(f)$ is bounded on $L^2(\phi)$ by Cauchy-Schwarz, so Riesz-Frechet gives $g$ with $\lambda(f)=\phi(fg)$. Testing on indicators and using Lemma 4.4 (averages) gives $0\le g\le1$ a.e. The set $B=\{g=1\}$ is $\mu$-null, which splits $\lambda=\lambda_a+\lambda_s$ with $\lambda_s\perp\mu$. Rewriting as $\lambda((1-g)f)=\mu(fg)$ and testing with $f=1_{A\cap E}(1+g+\dots+g^{n-1})$, dominated and monotone convergence give $\lambda_a(E)=\mu(1_Eh)$ with $h=1_Ag/(1-g)$. The $\sigma$-finite case is by partition, then signed and complex by decomposition.

records.proofSketch: Take σ-finite (X,μ) and (Y,ν). Define μ×ν on measurable rectangles by μ(A)ν(B) and extend it by Carathéodory to the product σ-algebra. A monotone-class (π–λ) argument shows that for every measurable E the sections E_x are measurable and x↦ν(E_x) is measurable, and that E↦∫ν(E_x)dμ(x) and E↦∫μ(E^y)dν(y) are measures agreeing with μ×ν on rectangles; σ-finiteness and uniqueness of extension from a π-system make them equal to μ×ν. Passing from indicators to nonnegative simple functions and then to monotone limits gives Tonelli, and Fubini follows from the positive and negative parts.

records.proofSketch: Specialize to Lebesgue measure on ℝ^{m+n}, where regularity can replace the π–λ argument. An open set U is a countable disjoint union of half-open dyadic boxes, so |U|=∫|U_x|dx by countable additivity and monotone convergence. Decreasing limits of open sets of finite measure give G_δ sets (dominated convergence), and every null set sits inside a null G_δ set, so almost every section of a null set is null. Outer regularity then covers all Lebesgue-measurable E, with almost every section measurable, and simple-function approximation gives Tonelli and Fubini for the completed measure.

records.proofSketch: For f,f̂∈L¹ and ε>0, Fubini and the self-dual Gaussian transform give ∫f̂(ξ)e^{2πixξ}e^{−πε²ξ²}dξ=(f∗G_ε)(x), where G_ε(t)=ε^{−1}e^{−πt²/ε²} is an approximate identity. As ε→0 the left side tends to ∫f̂(ξ)e^{2πixξ}dξ by dominated convergence (f̂∈L¹), while the right side tends to f(x) at each continuity point of f because G_ε concentrates at 0 and f∈L¹. Hence the inversion formula holds at continuity points.

records.routeTitle: inversion via contour or Fourier integrals
records.proofSketch: Truncate the inverse integral: S_R(x)=∫_{−R}^{R}f̂(ξ)e^{2πixξ}dξ=∫f(y)sin(2πR(x−y))/(π(x−y))dy, by Fubini and direct integration of the exponential. Since f̂∈L¹, S_R(x) converges as R→∞ to the full inverse integral. Averaging S_ρ over ρ∈[0,R] replaces the Dirichlet kernel by the Fejér kernel sin²(πRt)/(π²Rt²), a positive approximate identity (its total mass, ∫sin²u/u²du=π, can be computed by contour integration), so the averages tend to f(x) at continuity points of f. A convergent family and its Cesàro averages have the same limit, so the inverse integral equals f(x).

records.routeTitle: Parseval identity on a dense class plus completion
records.proofSketch: On the Schwartz class 𝒮 the transform maps 𝒮 to itself, and the multiplication formula ∫f̂g=∫fĝ together with inversion on 𝒮 gives ⟨f̂,ĝ⟩=⟨f,g⟩, so ‖f̂‖₂=‖f‖₂. Since 𝒮 is dense in L², the transform extends uniquely to a linear isometry of L². Its range is closed and contains 𝒮, hence is all of L², so the extension is unitary; on L¹∩L² it agrees with the integral formula by approximation.

records.proofSketch: Prove the isometry on L¹∩L² directly with Gaussian damping, without using inversion. For f∈L¹∩L², Fubini gives ∫|f̂(ξ)|²e^{−πεξ²}dξ=∫∫f(x)\overline{f(y)}ε^{−1/2}e^{−π(x−y)²/ε}dx dy=⟨f,f∗G_ε⟩, with G_ε a Gaussian approximate identity. Let ε↓0: the left side increases to ‖f̂‖₂² by monotone convergence and the right side tends to ‖f‖₂² because f∗G_ε→f in L². Hence the transform is isometric on L¹∩L², extends by density to L², and the identity F²f(x)=f(−x) on 𝒮 shows the extension is onto.

records.proofSketch: Translations τ_a on L²(ℝ) form a strongly continuous unitary group of commuting operators. By Stone's theorem and the spectral theorem for commuting unitaries (SNAG), this action is unitarily equivalent to multiplication by e^{−2πiaξ} on L²(ℝ̂,ν) for a spectral measure ν on the dual line, and the unitary intertwiner plays the role of the Fourier transform. The remaining work is to identify ν with Lebesgue measure and to show multiplicity one, for instance by testing against the Gaussian; this sketch does not carry that out.

records.proofSketch: Parametrize a smooth simple closed curve by arclength with length L and enclosed area A. A maximizing curve exists after compactness/regularization; first variation of A−λL shows its curvature is constant, hence the optimizer is a circle. Its area is L²/(4π), giving A≤L²/(4π). The existence and regularity step is essential and is not supplied by the Euler–Lagrange calculation alone.

records.proofSketch: Rescale so the curve has length L=2π and parametrize by arclength s as a smooth closed curve (x(s),y(s)). Expand x=Σaₙeⁱⁿˢ and y=Σbₙeⁱⁿˢ. Parseval gives Σn²(|aₙ|²+|bₙ|²)=(1/2π)∫(x′²+y′²)ds=1, while A=∫x y′ ds=2π·Σ i n āₙbₙ (integration by parts, since ∫y x′=−∫x y′). Hence A ≤ 2πΣ|n||aₙ||bₙ| ≤ πΣ|n|(|aₙ|²+|bₙ|²) ≤ πΣn²(|aₙ|²+|bₙ|²)=π=L²/4π. Equality forces aₙ=bₙ=0 for |n|≥2 and |a₁|=|b₁| with the right phase, i.e. a circle (Hurwitz).

records.proofSketch: Repeatedly Steiner-symmetrize a bounded region: each symmetrization preserves area and does not increase perimeter. A compactness argument gives a limit invariant under every direction of symmetrization, hence a disk; lower semicontinuity of perimeter shows the disk has no larger perimeter than the original region. This proves Per(E)≥2√(π|E|), with equality only for disks up to null sets.

records.proofSketch: Hadwiger–Ohmann slicing. For boxes with sides a_i, b_i the inequality is AM–GM applied to ∏a_i/(a_i+b_i) and ∏b_i/(a_i+b_i). For finite unions of boxes, induct on the total number of boxes: if A has at least two boxes, a coordinate hyperplane separates two of them; cut A into A⁺ and A⁻ with fewer boxes, translate B so the same hyperplane splits B in the same volume ratio, apply induction to the pairs (A^±,B^±) and add. Approximate compact sets from outside by decreasing finite unions of boxes and pass to the limit; measurable sets follow by inner approximation with compact sets.

records.proofSketch: Knothe–Rosenblatt transport. For compact A,B of positive volume let T:A→B be the triangular monotone map pushing the normalized uniform measure on A to that on B; its Jacobian determinant is constant, equal to |B|/|A|, and since DT is triangular with nonnegative diagonal entries t_1,…,t_n, we have ∏t_i=|B|/|A|. The map x↦x+T(x) is injective on A with image inside A+B and Jacobian ∏(1+t_i)≥(1+(∏t_i)^{1/n})^n by AM–GM. Hence |A+B|≥|A|(1+(|B|/|A|)^{1/n})^n=(|A|^{1/n}+|B|^{1/n})^n. The lack of smoothness of T is handled by approximation.

records.proofSketch: Prékopa–Leindler: if h((1−λ)x+λy)≥f(x)^{1−λ}g(y)^λ then ∫h≥(∫f)^{1−λ}(∫g)^λ (proved by induction on dimension from the one-dimensional case by monotone rearrangement). Apply it with f=1_A, g=1_B, h=1_{(1−λ)A+λB} to get |(1−λ)A+λB|≥|A|^{1−λ}|B|^λ. Normalize A′=A/α and B′=B/β with α=|A|^{1/n}, β=|B|^{1/n}, so |A′|=|B′|=1, and take λ=β/(α+β): then (1−λ)A′+λB′=(A+B)/(α+β), giving |A+B|≥(α+β)ⁿ.

records.entryName: Carathéodory's theorem for convex hulls in Rᵈ
records.proofSketch: Cast the representation as a linear program: find λ≥0 with Σλ_i x_i=x and Σλ_i=1, which has d+1 equality constraints in the variables λ_1,…,λ_m. The feasible set is nonempty (x∈conv) and lies in the nonnegative orthant, so it is a pointed polyhedron and has a vertex. A vertex is a basic feasible solution, whose support has linearly independent constraint columns, hence at most d+1 elements.

records.proofSketch: Induct on the number m of points used. For m≤d+1 there is nothing to prove. For m>d+1 the points are affinely dependent in ℝ^d, so Σa_i x_i=0 and Σa_i=0 with some a_j>0. records.proofSketch: Take a minimal subfamily C_1,…,C_k with empty intersection. By hypothesis k≥d+2, and by minimality each ∩_{j≠i}C_j is nonempty, so pick x_i in it. These k≥d+2 points of ℝ^d are affinely dependent: Σa_ix_i=0, Σa_i=0, not all a_i zero. Split the indices into P={a_i>0} and N={a_i<0}; the point p=Σ_P a_ix_i/Σ_P a_i=Σ_N(−a_i)x_i/Σ_N(−a_i) lies in both convex hulls. For each j, either j∉P or j∉N, so all x_i of that class lie in C_j and p∈C_j by convexity. Thus p∈∩C_j, a contradiction. This inlines Radon's theorem instead of inducting on the family size.

records.proofSketch: Nerve route. In a finite family of convex sets every nonempty intersection is contractible, so the nerve N is homotopy equivalent to the union (nerve lemma), and likewise for every subfamily. A union of compact convex sets in ℝ^d has vanishing reduced homology in degrees ≥d (Alexander duality), so every induced subcomplex of N does too (the d-Leray property). If every d+1 sets meet, N has a complete d-skeleton. If N were not a full simplex, a minimal non-face σ with |σ|=k+1≥d+2 would give the induced subcomplex ∂Δ^k, which has H̃_{k−1}≠0 with k−1≥d, contradicting the Leray bound. This is the route that generalizes to topological, colorful and fractional Helly theorems.

records.entryName: Radon's theorem for finite point sets
records.proofSketch: Suppose, for contradiction, every partition of d+2 points into two parts has disjoint convex hulls. Strict separation then supplies a hyperplane separating each pair of hulls. The sign patterns of these separating affine functionals cannot realize all required dichotomies of d+2 points in R^d (affine halfspaces have VC dimension d+1); therefore some partition has intersecting hulls. This is a separation-theorem proof of Radon, but it is less elementary and its separation/dimension argument must be stated fully.

records.proofSketch: Write max flow as a linear program in the arc flows x_e with 0≤x_e≤c_e and conservation at inner vertices. Its dual assigns potentials p_v with p_t−p_s≥1 and arc variables y_{uv}≥max(0,p_v−p_u), minimizing Σc_ey_e. Strong LP duality equates the two optima. The constraint matrix is a network matrix, hence totally unimodular, so the dual has an optimal solution that is integral with potentials in {0,1} after shifting p_s=0; the set S={v: p_v=0} then defines an s–t cut whose capacity equals the dual value.

records.proofSketch: Add a return arc t→s of unbounded capacity: flows of value k correspond to circulations carrying k on this arc. By Hoffman's circulation theorem (itself a consequence of Farkas' lemma), a feasible circulation with lower bound k on the return arc exists iff every vertex set S has (lower bounds into S) ≤ (upper bounds out of S); testing sets with s∈S, t∉S says exactly that every s–t cut has capacity ≥k. The polyhedron of circulations has a totally unimodular constraint matrix, so integer capacities give an integral maximum flow.

records.proofSketch: Kirchhoff's route: regard G as a network of unit resistors. Potentials φ for a unit current from u to v solve Lφ=e_u−e_v, and Cramer's rule gives the effective resistance R_{uv}=det L̂_{(u,v)}/det L̂_{(u)}, with one or two rows and columns deleted. The deletion–contraction recursion τ(G)=τ(G−e)+τ(G/e) for spanning-tree counts is matched by the matrix determinant lemma det(M+bbᵀ)=det M+bᵀadj(M)b applied to L̂(G)=L̂(G−e)+bbᵀ, whose second term is det L̂(G/e). Induction on edges (allowing disconnected graphs, where both sides vanish) then gives det L̂=τ(G).

records.proofSketch: Use Chaiken's all-minors extension. Write L=NNᵀ with N an oriented vertex–edge incidence matrix. records.routeTitle: Finite-subset compactness/König lemma for countable locally finite cases
records.proofSketch: Let (A_i)_{i∈I} be finite sets satisfying Hall's condition on every finite subfamily. For finite F⊂I let X_F⊂∏A_i be the set of choice functions injective on F: X_F is nonempty by the finite Hall theorem and closed in the product of finite discrete spaces. Since X_F∩X_G⊇X_{F∪G}, the family has the finite intersection property, and Tychonoff compactness gives a point of ∩X_F, an injective choice function. For countable families, König's lemma or diagonal extraction replaces Tychonoff. Finiteness of each A_i is essential.

records.routeTitle: choice/Zorn argument under stated cardinal assumptions
records.proofSketch: Zorn on shrinking the sets, assuming each A_i is finite. Order the families (A′_i)_{i∈I} with A′_i⊆A_i satisfying Hall's condition by reverse inclusion. A chain has a lower bound (intersect along the chain): each finite subfamily involves finitely many finite sets, on which the chain stabilizes, so Hall's condition survives. A minimal family has every |A′_i|=1: if a≠b lie in A′_i, deleting either would violate Hall, giving two tight subfamilies, and the standard Halmos–Vaughan counting argument on their union and intersection yields a contradiction. The singletons then form an SDR. Without finiteness of the A_i this fails.

records.entryName: Kruskal's theorem (finite graphs have finite obstruction sets under the minor relation)
records.proofSketch: Prove Kruskal's tree theorem via Higman's lemma: finite words over a well-quasi-order are well-quasi-ordered by subsequence embedding. In a minimal bad sequence of trees, the set of proper subtrees that occur is well-quasi-ordered by minimality, so by Higman the words of subtrees are well-quasi-ordered; this yields i<j with T_i embeddable in T_j. Tree embedding is a special case of the minor relation, so this gives well-quasi-order for finite forests under minors, which is much weaker than the graph-minor theorem.

records.entryName: Kruskal's theorem (finite graphs have finite obstruction sets under the minor relation)
records.proofSketch: The statement for arbitrary finite graphs is the Robertson–Seymour graph-minor theorem, whose proof is structural rather than algebraic. Outline: take a minimal bad sequence G_1,G_2,…; since G_1 is not a minor of any later G_j, all G_j with j≥2 exclude G_1 as a minor. The graph-minor structure theorem describes such graphs as clique-sums of pieces that are nearly embeddable in a surface of bounded genus, with a bounded number of apices and vortices of bounded width. Well-quasi-order for these pieces, via tree decompositions and a labelled-minor strengthening, then yields a contradiction (Graph Minors XX). Only this outline is given; the full argument spans many long papers.

records.proofSketch: Local-degree route. For x∈U choose a closed ball B⊂U around x; K=f(B) is homeomorphic to a ball, so its complement in Sⁿ is acyclic (an Alexander-duality lemma, quoted rather than reproved). This identifies the local homology H_n(B,B∖x)≅ℤ with H_n(ℝⁿ,ℝⁿ∖f(x))≅ℤ, so f has local degree ±1 at x. Combining this with the acyclicity shows that f(x) cannot be a boundary point of f(B); the details of that step are the standard Alexander-duality argument and are not reproduced here. Hence f(U) is open, and f is an open injective map, so a homeomorphism onto its image. The sign of the local degree is locally constant.

records.routeTitle: contradiction using compactness and boundary/sphere separation
records.proofSketch: Jordan–Brouwer route. Fix a closed ball B⊂U and set Σ=f(∂B)≅S^{n−1}. By Jordan–Brouwer separation ℝⁿ∖Σ has exactly two components, a bounded C_in and an unbounded C_out. The compact set f(B) is homeomorphic to a ball, so it does not separate ℝⁿ: ℝⁿ∖f(B) is connected, unbounded and lies in ℝⁿ∖Σ, hence lies in C_out. Therefore C_in⊆f(B)∖Σ=f(int B). Conversely f(int B) is connected and disjoint from Σ, so it lies in one component, which must be C_in since C_in⊆f(int B). Thus f(int B)=C_in is open. As balls around any point work, f is an open map and so a homeomorphism onto f(U).

records.entryName: Euler characteristic of a finite chain complex equals alternating homology dimension
records.proofSketch: Over a chain complex of vector spaces, write $Z_k=\ker\partial_k$ and $B_k=\operatorname{im}\partial_{k+1}$. Since $H_k=Z_k/B_k$ one has $\dim Z_k=\dim H_k+\dim B_k$. Because $\partial^2=0$, $C_k/Z_k\cong B_{k-1}$, so $\dim C_k=\dim Z_k+\dim B_{k-1}$. Combining, $\dim C_k=\dim H_k+\dim B_k+\dim B_{k-1}$. Multiply by $(-1)^k$ and sum over $k$; the boundary terms telescope, leaving $\sum(-1)^k\dim C_k=\sum(-1)^k\dim H_k$.

records.entryName: Euler characteristic of a finite chain complex equals alternating homology dimension
records.proofSketch: For a chain complex of finitely generated abelian groups with cycles $Z_n$, boundaries $B_n$ and homology $H_n=Z_n/B_n$ there are short exact sequences $0\to Z_n\to C_n\to B_{n-1}\to 0$ and $0\to B_n\to Z_n\to H_n\to 0$. Additivity of rank on short exact sequences gives $\operatorname{rank}C_n=\operatorname{rank}Z_n+\operatorname{rank}B_{n-1}$ and $\operatorname{rank}Z_n=\operatorname{rank}B_n+\operatorname{rank}H_n$. Substitute, multiply by $(-1)^n$ and sum: boundary ranks cancel, giving $\sum(-1)^n\operatorname{rank}C_n=\sum(-1)^n\operatorname{rank}H_n$. Applied to cellular chains this gives $\chi(X)=\sum(-1)^n\operatorname{rank}H_n(X)$.

records.proofSketch: Look for a maximal subset of A that f carries compatibly. Call X⊆A admissible if g(B∖f(X))∩X=∅, i.e. no point of X is the g-image of an element outside f(X). Admissible sets are closed under arbitrary unions, so there is a largest one, X₀. Maximality forces X₀=A∖g(B∖f(X₀)): otherwise a point outside both could be added to X₀. Define h=f on X₀ and h=g^{−1} on A∖X₀=g(B∖f(X₀)). Then h is injective and its image is f(X₀)∪(B∖f(X₀))=B.

records.proofSketch: View the construction as a fixed point. Φ(X)=A∖g(B∖f(X)) is monotone on the complete lattice 𝒫(A), so by the Knaster–Tarski theorem it has a fixed point X₀=Φ(X₀) (its greatest fixed point is the maximal admissible set of the previous route). The identity A∖X₀=g(B∖f(X₀)) is Banach's decomposition lemma: A splits as X₀⊔g(B′) and B as f(X₀)⊔B′ with B′=B∖f(X₀). Gluing f on X₀ with g^{−1} on g(B′) gives the bijection. The same argument runs in complete Boolean algebras (the Sikorski–Tarski versions), which is the form used for generalizations.

records.proofSketch: Systematic tableaux. Enlarge the language by countably many fresh constants and fix a fair order of rule applications, so every non-literal formula on a branch is eventually expanded and every universal formula is instantiated at every closed term. If the tableau for Σ∪{¬φ} stays open, a finished or infinite open branch is a Hintikka set, and its closed-term model satisfies all its formulas by induction on complexity. Hence Σ∪{¬φ} has a model; contrapositively, if Σ⊨φ every systematic tableau closes, and a closed tableau converts into a proof.

records.proofSketch: Gentzen-style route in the cut-free sequent calculus LK. Given Γ⇒Δ, search for a proof bottom-up, applying every rule systematically (instantiating ∀-left and ∃-right at all terms, and using fresh constants for the eigenvariable rules). If every branch closes, the search yields a cut-free proof; otherwise an open branch defines a countermodel, with its atoms true on the left and false on the right (Schütte's semantic argument). Cut elimination (Gentzen's Hauptsatz) shows cut-free LK is no weaker than LK with cut, so completeness transfers to the usual formulations of provability.

records.entryName: Gödel's incompleteness theorem (first theorem, standard effective theories)
records.proofSketch: Fix a Gödel numbering and an effectively axiomatized theory T interpreting enough arithmetic (Robinson's Q) that recursive relations, in particular the proof predicate Prf_T(y,x), are representable. The diagonal lemma gives a sentence G with T⊢G↔¬∃y Prf_T(y,⌜G⌝), 'I am not provable'. If T⊢G, a proof exists, so T⊢∃y Prf_T(y,⌜G⌝) and hence T⊢¬G: T is inconsistent. So for consistent T, G is unprovable. If T⊢¬G, T proves that G has a proof, while no actual proof exists; ω-consistency forbids this. Hence G is independent of T. (Gödel's argument needs ω-consistency for the second half; Rosser removes it.)

records.entryName: Gödel's incompleteness theorem (first theorem, standard effective theories)
records.proofSketch: Rosser's trick: apply the diagonal lemma to 'if I have a proof, a smaller proof of my negation exists', giving a sentence R with T⊢R↔∀y(Prf_T(y,⌜R⌝)→∃z≤y Prf_T(z,⌜¬R⌝)). If T⊢R with proof number n, then T proves Prf(n̄,⌜R⌝) and hence ∃z≤n̄ Prf(z,⌜¬R⌝); but consistency means ¬R has no proof, so T proves ¬Prf(k̄,⌜¬R⌝) for each k≤n, a contradiction. If T⊢¬R with proof number m, then T proves Prf(m̄,⌜¬R⌝), so the bound is witnessed for every y>m, while for y≤m the bounded instances Prf(y,⌜R⌝) are refutable; hence T⊢R and T is inconsistent. Only plain consistency of T is used.

records.entryName: Gödel's incompleteness theorem (first theorem, standard effective theories)
records.proofSketch: Recursion-theoretic form: suppose T is consistent, effectively axiomatized and represents all recursive functions, so true Σ₁ sentences are provable. Take the recursively inseparable r.e. sets A={e: φ_e(e)=0} and B={e: φ_e(e)=1}. If T decided every sentence 'φ_e(e)=0', the set {e: T⊢'φ_e(e)=0'} would be recursive (search for a proof of the sentence or its negation), would contain A by Σ₁-completeness, and would be disjoint from B by consistency, separating A from B, which is impossible. So some sentence of this form is undecided by T. This gives incompleteness but not the explicit Gödel sentence or the second incompleteness theorem.

records.entryName: Fundamental theorem of arithmetic for algebraic number fields fails in general; ideal factorization restores uniqueness
records.proofSketch: In the ring of integers O_K of a number field, show O_K is a Dedekind domain: it is Noetherian, integrally closed, and every nonzero prime ideal is maximal. For a nonzero ideal I, localize at each nonzero prime P; the DVR O_{K,P} gives I_P=P^{v_P(I)}O_{K,P}. Only finitely many exponents are nonzero, and equality can be checked after localization, giving the unique factorization I=∏P^{v_P(I)}.

records.entryName: Fundamental theorem of arithmetic for algebraic number fields fails in general; ideal factorization restores uniqueness
records.proofSketch: Localize O_K at each nonzero prime ideal P. The local ring is a discrete valuation ring, so every nonzero ideal becomes P^{v_P(I)} locally. The exponents v_P(I) are uniquely determined and vanish for all but finitely many P; intersecting the local equalities recovers I=∏P^{v_P(I)}. This is the local-valuation form of the same ideal-factorization proof, not an independent theorem-level result.

records.entryName: Finite subgroups of a field's multiplicative group are cyclic
records.routeTitle: Choose an element of maximum order and use polynomial root bounds
records.proofSketch: Let $G$ be a finite subgroup of $F^\times$. In a finite abelian group, elements of orders $n_1,n_2$ yield an element of order $\operatorname{lcm}(n_1,n_2)$. Hence if $n$ is the maximal element order, every element order divides $n$. So every element of $G$ is a root of $X^n-1$, giving $\#G\le n$ since a polynomial has at most $\deg$ roots in a field. Also $n$ divides $\#G$ by Lagrange, so $n=\#G$ and some element has order $\#G$, i.e. $G$ is cyclic.

records.entryName: Finite subgroups of a field's multiplicative group are cyclic
records.routeTitle: classify finite abelian groups and compare exponent with group size
records.proofSketch: All proofs rest on the fact that $x^d=1$ has at most $d$ solutions in a field. Using the structure theorem for finite abelian groups: if $|G|=n$ and $G$ is not cyclic, the invariant-factor decomposition gives a $d<n$ (the exponent) with $x^d=1$ for all $x\in G$. That gives more than $d$ roots of $x^d-1$, a contradiction, so $G$ is cyclic.

records.entryName: Uniformization theorem for simply connected Riemann surfaces
records.proofSketch: Potential-theoretic route. Exhaust X by relatively compact regular domains and use Perron's method for the Dirichlet problem to decide whether X carries a Green's function. If it does (hyperbolic case), take the Green's function g with a logarithmic pole at p; X simply connected gives a harmonic conjugate g*, so F=exp(−(g+ig*)) is a single-valued holomorphic map X→𝔻, which one shows to be bijective. If X is non-compact without a Green's function, a harmonic function with a single logarithmic pole at p and controlled growth gives a biholomorphism onto ℂ; compact X is handled separately by producing a meromorphic function with one simple pole (Dirichlet principle), mapping X onto the Riemann sphere. The parabolic and compact cases are only indicated here.

records.entryName: Uniformization theorem for simply connected Riemann surfaces
records.proofSketch: Riemann-mapping-style extremal argument for the hyperbolic case. Fix p∈X and consider the family 𝓕 of injective holomorphic maps h:X→𝔻 with h(p)=0; assume 𝓕≠∅ (a first such map comes from a Green's function or an embedding theorem). Montel's theorem makes 𝓕 normal, and a maximizer of |h′(p)| exists, injective by Hurwitz. If the maximizer missed a point of 𝔻, Koebe's square-root-and-Möbius construction would give a map in 𝓕 with larger derivative at p, a contradiction; so the maximizer is a biholomorphism onto 𝔻. The cases ℂ and the sphere need a different argument.

records.entryName: Uniformization theorem for simply connected Riemann surfaces
records.proofSketch: Ricci-flow route (Hamilton, Chow) for the compact case. On a compact surface evolve the metric by the normalized Ricci flow ∂_tg=(r̄−R)g. Hamilton proved long-time existence and convergence to a constant-curvature metric when the Euler characteristic is ≤0, and Chow completed the case χ>0 (the sphere). The limit metric is conformal to the original, and the universal cover of a constant-curvature surface is the sphere, the plane or the disk with its model metric. Non-compact simply connected surfaces such as ℂ and 𝔻 are not covered by this sketch.
